title: Bangladesh Presses India to Speed Up Sheikh Hasina Extradition
excerpt: Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi said New Delhi cannot commit to a timeline, stressing that the extradition request is being examined through an established legal process under the bilateral treaty.
body:
• Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi told the Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka on October 3 that India cannot give any timeline for a decision on Bangladesh's request to extradite former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina: "Nobody can give you a time frame."
  • The request is being examined through the established legal process under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty of 2013, amended in 2016 — not through a political decision.
  • Trivedi said India had "hardly any choice" but to receive Hasina in August 2024, describing "tragic circumstances" in which New Delhi neither brought her to India nor was prepared for her arrival.
  • To watch: any decision will follow treaty legal procedures and court involvement; Dhaka's government led by Tarique Rahman wants the process expedited so Hasina can face charges at home.

Bangladesh has asked India to speed up the extradition of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, and India has answered: the process is legal, the courts are involved, and no one can say when it will end.

Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi laid out New Delhi's position at the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026 in Dhaka on October 3, in the first detailed public explanation of why the extradition request — formally submitted by Dhaka — remains unresolved more than two years after Hasina fled to India.

"There is a process, and the process involves legality. And it is very structured. As far as that is concerned, the process is on. And the courts are involved. So nobody can give you a time frame."

— Dinesh Trivedi, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh

"Hardly any choice" but to receive her

Trivedi addressed the most sensitive part of the story head-on: how Hasina ended up in India at all. He said the country had "hardly any choice" but to allow the aircraft carrying her to land in August 2024, when her government collapsed amid a mass uprising and she fled to safety.

"At that point in time, Hasina Ji was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that. It was our duty as a neighbour to accept the reality of life," he said, describing the "tragic circumstances" of her arrival. India, he stressed, neither brought her nor had prepared for her arrival — it responded to events.

The framing is a deliberate pushback against the narrative in parts of Bangladeshi politics that New Delhi sheltered Hasina by choice. It also echoes earlier Indian statements that the decision to let her enter was made on humanitarian and security grounds amid a rapidly deteriorating situation.

The legal process, and why it is slow

The extradition request is governed by the bilateral extradition treaty India and Bangladesh signed in 2013 and amended in 2016. The treaty creates a legal framework for handing over fugitives but also sets out grounds on which a request may be refused, including provisions relating to political offences.

Indian authorities have repeatedly said the request is "under examination" through established legal and diplomatic channels. Trivedi's comments make explicit what that means in practice: the matter sits with the legal system, and the courts will be involved. Any decision — to extradite or to refuse — must follow the treaty's procedures rather than a political directive, which is why New Delhi insists no executive timeline can be promised.

The government of Bangladesh, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman after the Bangladesh Nationalist Party's victory in the February 12 elections, has renewed the demand. In August, Dhaka raised the request during Rahman's meeting with Trivedi, with the Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary saying, "Bangladesh hopes that India will expedite the process of extraditing Sheikh Hasina." Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said Hasina, 79, would be arrested immediately if she returned, and that the court verdict against her would be implemented.

Beyond one case: a relationship under strain

The extradition issue has become the sharpest test of India-Bangladesh ties under the new government in Dhaka. Trivedi used the Dhaka platform to argue the relationship is bigger than any single dispute. "The Bangladesh-India relationship is more than transactional, it is cultural. A good neighbour always comes out in support of each other," he said, adding that India had "full confidence" in the people of Bangladesh.

He also addressed regional security, calling Bangladesh an independent and sovereign country capable of assessing its own security interests. The two countries continue to cooperate on trade, energy connectivity, cross-border infrastructure, and border management even as the extradition file remains open.

Why it matters for the region's Indians

The extradition standoff shapes the trajectory of India-Bangladesh relations — ties that touch the millions of people with family, business, and cultural connections across the border, and the flow of trade, travel, and remittances between the two countries. How the legal process resolves will set the tone for the bilateral relationship for years.

What to watch

There is no announced timeline and no indication of one coming. The watch items are procedural: whether India's legal examination reaches a formal decision, whether Dhaka escalates through other channels, and whether the issue surfaces in upcoming bilateral meetings. For now, the file sits with the lawyers — and both governments are managing the politics around it.
